'''''Arbutus xalapensis''''', commonly known as the '''Texas madrone''', '''Amazaquitl''', or '''Texas madroño''',<ref>[https://www.wildflower.org/plants/result.php?id_plant=arxa80 Ladybird Johnson Wildflower Center]</ref> is a species of [[flowering plant]] in the [[Erica (plant)|heather]] family. It is native to [[Central America]], the [[southwestern United States]] (western [[Texas]] and [[New Mexico]]), and throughout [[Mexico]].<ref>[http://bonap.net/MapGallery/County/Arbutus%20xalapensis.png Biota of North America Program 2014 county distribution map]</ref><ref>[http://swbiodiversity.org/seinet/taxa/index.php?taxon=17908 SEINet, Southwestern Biodiversity, Arizona chapter] photos, description, distribution map</ref> It is found in canyons and mountains, on rocky plains, and in oak woodlands, at altitudes of up to {{convert|3,000|m|ft|abbr=on}} in the south of the range, but lower, down to {{convert|600|m|ft|abbr=on}} in the north of the range.

''Arbutus xalapensis'' is a large [[shrub]] or small to medium-sized [[evergreen]] [[tree]] growing to {{convert|5|–|25|m|ft|sp=us}} tall with a trunk up to {{convert|50|cm|in|abbr=on}} in diameter, with smooth orange-brown bark peeling in thin sheets. The size varies regionally with available rainfall, with small, shrubby plants in dry areas such as western Texas and New Mexico, and larger trees in moister areas of Mexico; plants in Texas, New Mexico, and the far northeast of Mexico are distinguished as a variety, ''A. xalapensis'' var. ''texana'', or even a distinct species ''A. texana'', by some botanists, but others do not regard these as distinct.<ref name=tammy>[http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=1&taxon_id=250092310 Flora of North America, ''Arbutus xalapensis'' Kunth, 1819. Texas madrone ]</ref>

The [[leaf|leaves]] are oblong to lanceolate, {{convert|5|–|17|cm|in|abbr=on}} long and {{convert|1.5|–|5|cm|in|abbr=on}} broad, with an entire or serrated margin. The [[flower]]s are bell-shaped, white or pale pink, 5–10 mm long, produced in loose [[panicle]]s. The [[fruit]] is a rough-surfaced red [[Berry (botany)|berry]] {{convert|1|cm|in|abbr=on}} in diameter, reportedly edible (however, those of related species have narcotic properties), and contains numerous small [[seed]]s.<ref name=tammy/><ref>{{cite book|last=Little|first=Elbert L.|title=The Audubon Society Field Guide to North American Trees: Eastern Region|publisher=Knopf|location=New York|year=1980|isbn=0-394-50760-6|page=622}}</ref>
